uncited: This family solves the problem of estimating surface normals and edge strength for volume rendering, segmentation, and physics simulation without requiring analytic derivatives or precomputed gradient volumes.

It is distinguished from [Analytic Gradient Computation](2167-analytic-gradient-computation.md) by its reliance on discrete sampling rather than closed-form differentiation, and from [Gradient Estimation from Samples](2180-gradient-estimation-from-samples.md) by its deterministic, grid-aligned stencil structure rather than stochastic or ray-based estimation.

All methods in this family approximate the partial derivative $\frac{\partial V}{\partial x_i}$ at a voxel center $\mathbf{p}$ using a linear combination of scalar field values $V(\mathbf{p}_k)$ at neighboring positions $\mathbf{p}_k$.
where $w_k$ are weights determined by the stencil geometry and step size $h$ (voxel spacing).
For isotropic grids with $h=1$, the weights are typically integers or simple fractions.
The gradient vector is assembled as $\nabla V = (G_x, G_y, G_z)$.
Finite difference methods are foundational in numerical analysis for approximating derivatives of functions defined on discrete grids.
In volume rendering, they are used to estimate surface normals for lighting calculations (e.g., Phong shading) and to detect edges for opacity transfer functions.
The central difference stencil is the most common due to its second-order accuracy and symmetry.
Forward and backward differences are used when computational efficiency is prioritized or when boundary conditions dictate asymmetric access.
Higher-order methods like 4th-order and WENO5 provide improved smoothness for ray marching and SDFs.
The method is widely used in scientific visualization, medical imaging, and real-time volume rendering engines.
